hints: Focus on how an ester is built, it is a carboxylic acid joined to an alcohol with water removed.
Notice the first part, CH3CO2, comes from ethanoic acid, so the rest, CH(CH3)CH2CH3, must come from alcohol Y.
Add an OH back onto that alcohol fragment where it joined to the acid, then name the resulting 4-carbon chain by numbering to give OH the lowest number.
walkthrough:
**Recall how esters form**

Think of esterification as acid + alcohol gives ester + water. The acid provides the acyl part and the alcohol provides the alkyl part joined through oxygen.

Chemical equation pattern:
$$\text{RCOOH} + \text{R'OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{RCOOR'} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Split ester X into its two parts**

Here the acid is ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, so the $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}$ part is from the acid. That leaves $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ as the group from alcohol Y.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COO- (from acid) + -CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \text{ (from alcohol)}$$

**Rebuild alcohol Y and name it**

Put the OH back where the alcohol joined to the acid to get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. This is a straight 4-carbon chain with OH on carbon 2, so it is butan-2-ol.

options.A: Incorrect. Butan-1-ol is CH3CH2CH2CH2OH, a primary alcohol. It would give the ester CH3CO2CH2CH2CH2CH3, not the branched attachment seen in X.
options.B: Correct. Replacing the ethanoate part with H gives CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3. Numbering to give OH the lowest locant gives butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol.
options.C: Incorrect. There is no such distinct name as butan-3-ol. By IUPAC numbering you always number to give the functional group the lowest number, so CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3 is butan-2-ol, not butan-3-ol.
options.D: Incorrect. Methylpropan-2-ol is (CH3)3COH, a tertiary branched alcohol with only 3 carbons in the longest chain. The alcohol fragment here is a straight 4-carbon chain, not branched.
